newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICANS DIVIDED ACROSS RACE ON STRIKES - SURVEY.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICANS DIVIDED ACROSS RACE ON STRIKES - SURVEY.

text.p: Most South African whites believe strikes take place too often and are managed too leniently, a survey by Market Research Africa showed on Monday.
They also think that the way the government handles labour issues is harming the economy. In contrast, a significant number of blacks surveyed said the opposite, the survey said.
"The huge gap between black and white thinking is clearly an area of concern," Market Research Africa director Brian Culross said in a statement.

"Whilst dramatic enough in itself, it emphasises the difficult task of the private sector and government to create labour policies which will satisfy workers and management without compromising productivity," Culross added.
The survey of 2,505 people excluding miners and live-in domestic workers on commission by Business Day from MRA in November last year.
On the frequency of strikes, 41 percent of those polled overall said workers behaved reasonably. But nine in 10 whites thought workers strike too often.
To a lesser extent, 55 percent of Indians and 48 percent of coloureds also thought the frequency of strikes unreasonable.
But nearly six in 10 blacks believed workers made judicious use of their right to strike, a view shared by only four percent of whites.
MRA said support for more strike activity was highest in Gauteng province at 10 percent, and the lowest at five percent in the job-starved Eastern Cape.

There was also divided opinion over the government's labour policies and actions. Overall 52 percent said its stance harmed the economy. Overwhelmingly this was the view among whites (85 percent) and an equal 52 percent among coloureds and Indians.
Blacks were divided with 37 percent saying the government's approach had a good effect on the economy, 37 percent believed it harmful, and 24 percent thought the economy unaffected.
